summary.text: At \(n=67\), the two distinct inputs \(147\) and \(2^{67}+1\) both give value \(67\): the residues of \(147\) modulo \(2,4,\ldots,128\) sum to \(1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67\), while each of the 67 relevant residues of \(2^{67}+1\) is 1. Thus there are at least two occurrences, contradicting the claimed uniqueness.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor \log_2 m\rfloor}(m\bmod 2^k)
\]
be sequence A049802, where \(m\bmod 2^k\) denotes the least nonnegative residue of \(m\) modulo \(2^k\). Thus \(a(n)\), sequence A383327, is the number of natural numbers \(m\) for which \(F(m)=n\).

We disprove the proposed assertion by considering the listed value \(n=67\). We will exhibit two distinct indices \(m\) at which A049802 is equal to \(67\).

First take \(m=147\). Since
\[
2^7=128\le 147<256=2^8,
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 147\rfloor=7\). The residues appearing in the definition of \(F(147)\) are therefore the residues modulo \(2,4,8,16,32,64,128\). They are
\[
\begin{aligned}
147\bmod 2&=1,\\
147\bmod 4&=3,\\
147\bmod 8&=3,\\
147\bmod 16&=3,\\
147\bmod 32&=19,\\
147\bmod 64&=19,\\
147\bmod 128&=19.
\end{aligned}
\]
Indeed, \(147=144+3\), which gives the residues modulo \(4,8,16\); also \(147=128+19\), which gives the residues modulo \(32,64,128\). Consequently,
\[
F(147)=1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67.
\]
Thus \(147\) is one occurrence of the value \(67\) in A049802.

There is also the usual “trivial” occurrence. Set
\[
M=2^{67}+1.
\]
We have
\[
2^{67}\le M<2^{68},
\]
because \(M=2^{67}+1\) and \(1<2^{67}\). Hence
\[
\lfloor\log_2 M\rfloor=67.
\]
For every integer \(k\) with \(1\le k\le 67\), the number \(2^k\) divides \(2^{67}\). Therefore
\[
M=2^{67}+1\equiv 1\pmod{2^k}.
\]
Since \(0\le 1<2^k\), its least nonnegative residue is exactly \(1\), so
\[
M\bmod 2^k=1
\qquad(1\le k\le 67).
\]
It follows that
\[
F(2^{67}+1)=\sum_{k=1}^{67}1=67.
\]
Thus \(2^{67}+1\) is a second occurrence of \(67\) in A049802.

These two indices are distinct. For example, \(2^{67}\ge 2^8=256>147\), so \(2^{67}+1>147\). Hence the set
\[
\{m:F(m)=67\}
\]
contains at least the two distinct elements \(147\) and \(2^{67}+1\). Therefore
\[
a(67)\ge 2,
\]
and in particular \(a(67)\ne 1\).

If one uses the finite counting formulation with the sufficient search range \(0\le m<2^{n+1}\), both witnesses are still counted when \(n=67\): clearly \(147<2^{68}\), and \(2^{67}+1<2^{68}\). Thus the same conclusion \(a(67)\ge2\) follows directly in that formulation as well.

Finally, \(67\) belongs to the proposed set
\[
\{1,3,5,9,15,23,35,63,65,67\}.
\]
The conjecture asserts that \(a(n)=1\) for every member of this set, so it would in particular imply \(a(67)=1\). This contradicts \(a(67)\ge2\). Therefore the conjecture is false.
